Sample.evidence_source: [page/6/Text/4] The respondents in the study were consecutively admitted attempted suicide patients, who agreed to participate in the study.

Country.evidence_source: [page/6/Text/4] For practical reasons, patients who could not understand Swedish were not asked to participate in the study (two patients during the period of data collection).

Population.evidence_source: [page/6/Text/4] The respondents in the study were consecutively admitted attempted suicide patients, who agreed to participate in the study. ... In this study, a majority of the respondents were male.

Type.evidence_source: [page/6/Text/6] The purpose of the original data collection was to explore experiences of psychiatric care after a suicide attempt.

Area.evidence_source: [page/5/Text/9] In this article, attempted suicide patients' shame reactions following a suicide attempt were highlighted. Many respondents described feelings of shame and sensitivity to the attitudes of the personnel at the time of admission to the hospital. Respondents' feelings of shame were sometimes alleviated or exacerbated during interaction with the hospital personnel. ... [page/6/Text/3] A tolerant and flexible atmosphere in the psychiatric ward, with low demands on the attempted suicide patients, helped them accept treatment and was perceived as alleviating the shame. ... [page/6/Text/8] Shame reactions may play an important role in restraining attempted suicide patients from seeking help. ... [page/6/Text/10] Shame reactions were common and threatened to restrain the patients from accepting admittance to hospital and from expressing their needs. Shame also made them sensitive to exposure situations and negative attitudes from the personnel. At the same time, experiencing the personnel as kind and respectful helped these patients to accept care and was perceived as alleviating feelings of shame.
